claim: The hippocampal theta rhythm plays important roles in information processing.
source: The hippocampal theta rhythm plays important roles in information processing; however, the mechanisms of its generation are not well understood.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature on hippocampal theta rhythms.

claim: The mechanisms of hippocampal theta rhythm generation are not well understood.
source: The hippocampal theta rhythm plays important roles in information processing; however, the mechanisms of its generation are not well understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as acknowledged by the authors.

claim: A data-driven, supercomputer-based, full-scale (1:1) model of the rodent CA1 area was developed.
source: We developed a data-driven, supercomputer-based, full-scale (1:1) model of the rodent CA1 area and studied its interneurons during theta oscillations.
evidence: The development of the model is described in the Methods section and demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Theta rhythm with phase-locked gamma oscillations spontaneously emerged from the isolated CA1 circuit without rhythmic inputs.
source: Theta rhythm with phase-locked gamma oscillations and phase-preferential discharges of distinct interneuronal types spontaneously emerged from the isolated CA1 circuit without rhythmic inputs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3 and 4 showing theta and gamma oscillations in the model.

claim: Phase-preferential discharges of distinct interneuronal types spontaneously emerged from the isolated CA1 circuit without rhythmic inputs.
source: Theta rhythm with phase-locked gamma oscillations and phase-preferential discharges of distinct interneuronal types spontaneously emerged from the isolated CA1 circuit without rhythmic inputs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing phase-preferential firing of different cell types.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons are important factors in theta generation.
source: Perturbation experiments identified parvalbumin-expressing interneurons and neurogliaform cells, as well as interneuronal diversity itself, as important factors in theta generation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing the effects of muting different cell types on theta oscillations.

claim: Neurogliaform cells are important factors in theta generation.
source: Perturbation experiments identified parvalbumin-expressing interneurons and neurogliaform cells, as well as interneuronal diversity itself, as important factors in theta generation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing the effects of muting different cell types on theta oscillations.

claim: Interneuronal diversity itself is an important factor in theta generation.
source: Perturbation experiments identified parvalbumin-expressing interneurons and neurogliaform cells, as well as interneuronal diversity itself, as important factors in theta generation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6E-F showing that reducing interneuronal diversity disrupts theta oscillations.

claim: The hippocampal CA1 area supports diverse cognitive tasks including learning, memory, and spatial processing.
source: The hippocampal CA1 area supports diverse cognitive tasks including learning, memory, and spatial processing (Squire, 1992; Remondes and Schuman, 2004; Manns et al., 2007; Moser et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental literature.

claim: Cognitive tasks in the hippocampus are thought to require coordination of neuronal activity provided by physiological network oscillations, including the theta rhythm.
source: These cognitive tasks are thought to require coordination of neuronal activity provided by physiological network oscillations, including the theta rhythm (Buzsáki, 2002; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: In rodents, hippocampal theta is a 5–10 Hz oscillation in the local field potential (LFP) and neuronal firing probabilities.
source: In rodents, hippocampal theta is a 5–10 Hz oscillation in the local field potential (LFP) and neuronal firing probabilities (Soltesz and Deschênes, 1993; Lee et al., 1994; Ylinen et al., 1995; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Varga et al., 2012, 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental literature.

claim: Hippocampal theta occurs during locomotion and in REM sleep.
source: In rodents, hippocampal theta is a 5–10 Hz oscillation in the local field potential (LFP) and neuronal firing probabilities (Soltesz and Deschênes, 1993; Lee et al., 1994; Ylinen et al., 1995; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Varga et al., 2012, 2014), occurring during locomotion and in REM sleep (Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to experimental literature.

claim: Several major afferents provide theta-frequency rhythmic input to the CA1 in vivo.
source: Though several major afferents provide theta-frequency rhythmic input to the CA1 in vivo (Soltesz and Deschênes, 1993; Buzsáki, 2002; Fuhrmann et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: Spontaneous theta-frequency LFP oscillations are present in the isolated whole CA1 preparation in vitro.
source: recent reports indicate the presence of spontaneous theta-frequency LFP oscillations even in the isolated whole CA1 preparation in vitro (Goutagny et al., 2009; Amilhon et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: The isolated CA1 preparation suggests an intrinsic ability of the CA1 circuit to generate some form of theta waves even without rhythmic external inputs.
source: Therefore, the latter studies suggest an intrinsic ability of the CA1 circuit to generate some form of theta waves even without rhythmic external inputs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental studies on isolated CA1 preparations.

claim: The intra-CA1 mechanisms that may contribute to the generation of the theta rhythm are not well understood.
source: However, the intra-CA1 mechanisms that may contribute to the generation of the theta rhythm are not well understood (Colgin, 2013, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review literature.

claim: Full-scale models advantageously avoid the connectivity scaling tradeoff that besets reduced-scale models.
source: In principle, such full-scale models of mammalian circuits comprising hundreds of thousands of neurons of distinct types advantageously avoid the connectivity scaling tradeoff that besets reduced-scale models
evidence: This is a theoretical advantage of full-scale models explained by the authors.

claim: Smaller models of large networks with realistic single cell electrophysiological properties remain silent unless synaptic strengths or numbers are arbitrarily increased beyond biologically relevant levels.
source: smaller models of large networks with realistic single cell electrophysiological properties (e.g., input resistance and resting membrane potential) remain silent unless synaptic strengths or numbers are arbitrarily increased beyond the biologically relevant levels to compensate for fewer inputs to their model cells (e.g., [Dyhrfjeld-Johnsen et al., 2007; Sterratt et al., 2011]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to modeling literature.

claim: Full-scale models require considerable computational resources.
source: However, full-scale models require considerable computational resources.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of full-scale computational models.

claim: Detailed models have a large parameter space which risks being sub-optimally constrained by neurobiological properties that are only partially quantified.
source: Further, such detailed models have a large parameter space which risks being sub-optimally constrained by neurobiological properties that are only partially quantified (Sejnowski et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to modeling literature.

claim: The CA1 area is one of the most extensively studied brain regions with abundant anatomical and electrophysiological data.
source: Because the CA1 area is one of the most extensively studied brain regions, there are abundant anatomical and electrophysiological data about its organization, making it a logical choice for the development of a full-scale model.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The CA1 area is a logical choice for the development of a full-scale model due to abundant data.
source: Because the CA1 area is one of the most extensively studied brain regions, there are abundant anatomical and electrophysiological data about its organization, making it a logical choice for the development of a full-scale model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the availability of data.

claim: The CA1 area supports diverse cognitive tasks that likely require the simultaneous processing of thousands of incoming and outgoing signals.
source: The CA1 area is also worth modeling at full-scale because of the diverse cognitive tasks it supports. These tasks likely require the simultaneous processing of thousands of incoming and outgoing signals
evidence: This is an inference about the computational requirements of CA1 function.

claim: Full-scale network models have the potential to match the in vivo processing capacity of the CA1.
source: and full-scale network models, at least in principle, have the potential to match this in vivo processing capacity.
evidence: This is a theoretical advantage of full-scale models.

claim: The simulated full-scale CA1 circuit was able to spontaneously generate theta waves as well as phase-locked gamma oscillations.
source: The simulated full-scale CA1 circuit was able to spontaneously generate theta waves as well as phase-locked gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Distinct interneuron types discharged at particular phases of theta, demonstrating that phase-preferential firing originates in part within the CA1 network.
source: Furthermore, distinct interneuron types discharged at particular phases of theta, demonstrating that phase-preferential firing (Klausberger et al., 2003, 2004, 2005; Ferraguti et al., 2005; Jinno et al., 2007; Fuentealba et al., 2008; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Varga et al., 2012; Lapray et al., 2012; Katona et al., 2014; Varga et al., 2014) originates in part within the CA1 network.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 and supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: Connections between CA1 pyramidal cells are important for theta generation.
source: Perturbation experiments revealed that parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons, neurogliaform cells, connections between CA1 pyramidal cells, and interneuronal diversity were important for theta generation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C showing the effects of altering pyramidal cell connections.

claim: The CA1 model network contained 338,740 cells, similar to the biological CA1 in rats.
source: The model network contained 338,740 cells (similar to the biological CA1 in rats, including 311,500 pyramidal cells and 27,240 interneurons) (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a specification of the model based on biological data.

claim: The CA1 model network included 311,500 pyramidal cells.
source: The model network contained 338,740 cells (similar to the biological CA1 in rats, including 311,500 pyramidal cells and 27,240 interneurons) (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a specification of the model based on biological data.

claim: The CA1 model network included 27,240 interneurons.
source: The model network contained 338,740 cells (similar to the biological CA1 in rats, including 311,500 pyramidal cells and 27,240 interneurons) (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a specification of the model based on biological data.

claim: The network incorporated 454,700 artificial stimulating cells to simulate afferents to CA1.
source: In addition, the network also incorporated 454,700 artificial stimulating cells (spiking units with random, Poisson-distributed interspike intervals) to simulate afferents to CA1
evidence: This is a specification of the model design.

claim: Cell type-specific connectivity data were taken without alteration from a previously published quantitative assessment of the CA1 circuit.
source: Cell type-specific connectivity data, including cell numbers (Figure 1D) and convergence and divergence values (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1) were taken without alteration from our previously published, in-depth, quantitative assessment of the CA1 circuit (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013).
evidence: This statement describes the source of connectivity data used in the model.

claim: The model network had a total of 5.19 billion synaptic connections.
source: for a total of 5.19 billion synaptic connections in the model network.
evidence: This is a specification of the model.

claim: For a four second simulation, the full-scale model required 3–4 terabytes (TB) of RAM.
source: For a four second simulation, the full-scale model required 3–4 terabytes (TB) of RAM and four hours of execution time on a supercomputer using ~3000 processors (or up to 12 hr for simulations calculating a high-accuracy local field potential (LFP) analog).
evidence: This is a specification of the computational requirements of the model.

claim: For a four second simulation, the full-scale model required four hours of execution time on a supercomputer using ~3000 processors.
source: For a four second simulation, the full-scale model required 3–4 terabytes (TB) of RAM and four hours of execution time on a supercomputer using ~3000 processors (or up to 12 hr for simulations calculating a high-accuracy local field potential (LFP) analog).
evidence: This is a specification of the computational requirements of the model.

claim: The pyramidal cell spikes exhibited peak power around the theta frequency of 7.8 Hz.
source: The pyramidal cell spikes (Figures 3C and D) exhibited peak power around the theta frequency of 7.8 Hz (Figure 4 and Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4 and Table 7.

claim: Theta was apparent within one theta period of the simulation start in all measures of network activity.
source: In all of these measures of network activity, theta was apparent within one theta period of the simulation start.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: The theta oscillation was stable, maintaining a steady power level throughout the duration of the oscillation.
source: The theta oscillation was stable, maintaining a steady power level throughout the duration of the oscillation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing the spectrogram.

claim: This is the first strictly data-driven, full-scale computational network model of the CA1 that exhibits spontaneous theta rhythm without rhythmic synaptic inputs.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first strictly data-driven, full-scale computational network model of the CA1 that exhibits spontaneous theta rhythm without rhythmic synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The model network displayed gamma oscillations (25–80 Hz).
source: In addition to theta rhythm, the model network displayed gamma oscillations (25–80 Hz; Figures 3B and 4D)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3B and 4D.

claim: The amplitude envelope of the gamma oscillation was phase-locked to the theta rhythm.
source: The amplitude envelope of the gamma oscillation was phase-locked to the theta rhythm (Figures 3A,B and 4C), as it is in the biological CA1, representing cross-frequency coupling (Soltesz and Deschênes, 1993; Bragin et al., 1995; Buzsáki et al., 2003; Jensen and Colgin, 2007; Belluscio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3A,B and 4C and supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: The highest amplitude of the gamma oscillations in the model was observed at the theta trough (0°/360°) in the pyramidal layer LFP analog.
source: The highest amplitude of the gamma oscillations in the model was observed at the theta trough (0°/360°) in the pyramidal layer LFP analog (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C.

claim: The model was sufficiently well-constrained by experimental data that it generated theta and gamma oscillations on its own, without extrinsic rhythmic inputs or deliberate tuning of intrinsic parameters.
source: These results demonstrate that, in spite of gaps in our knowledge, our model was sufficiently well-constrained by experimental data that it generated theta and gamma oscillations on its own, without extrinsic rhythmic inputs or deliberate tuning of intrinsic parameters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The pyramidal cells in the model tended to fire more than they typically do during theta oscillations in vivo.
source: Indeed, the pyramidal cells in our model described above (Figures 3 and 4) tended to fire more than they typically do during theta oscillations in vivo (e.g., [Soltesz and Deschênes, 1993; Robbe et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is an observation from the model compared to experimental data.

claim: In simulations with rationally scaled up inhibition, only 1% of the pyramidal cells were active, and they fired at a low rate of 1.8 Hz.
source: In simulations with the model containing this rationally scaled up inhibition, only 1% of the pyramidal cells were active, and they fired at a low rate of 1.8 Hz (data not shown), closely resembling the in vivo condition (Soltesz and Deschênes, 1993; Robbe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a result from additional simulations with modified parameters.

claim: The model was capable of reproducing the experimentally observed relatively low-firing frequencies for the principal cells during theta oscillations in vivo.
source: Therefore, the model was capable of reproducing the experimentally observed relatively low-firing frequencies for the principal cells during theta oscillations in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scaled inhibition simulations.

claim: The numerically dominant pyramidal cells preferentially discharged around the trough 0°/360° of the LFP analog theta rhythm.
source: As expected, the numerically dominant pyramidal cells, whose intracellular membrane potential oscillations to a large extent generate and underlie the extracellular LFP signal during theta oscillations (Buzsáki et al., 2012), preferentially discharged around the trough 0o/360o of the LFP analog theta rhythm (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A and supported by a citation.

claim: Phase-preferential firing emerged spontaneously from the full-scale model, without purposeful tuning of parameters except the mean spiking frequency and synaptic strength of the artificial stimulating cells.
source: Importantly, this fundamental property emerged spontaneously from the full-scale model, without purposeful tuning of parameters except the mean spiking frequency and synaptic strength of the artificial stimulating cells to set the incoming excitation levels from afferents (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a statement about the model design and results.

claim: The majority (71%; 5/7) of the interneuron types for which there were experimental data showed similar preferential maxima in their firing probabilities in the model and in vivo.
source: Specifically, the majority (71%; 5/7) of the interneuron types for which there were experimental data, including the CCK+ basket, axo-axonic, bistratified, O-LM and neurogliaform cells, showed similar preferential maxima in their firing probabilities in the model (Figure 5A) and in vivo (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The largest differences between the model and the in vivo phase-preferential firing occurred for the PV+ basket cells and the ivy cells.
source: The largest differences between the model and the in vivo phase-preferential firing occurred for the PV+ basket cells and the ivy cells
evidence: This is an observation from comparing model results to experimental data.

claim: During theta oscillations in vivo, PV+ basket cells and ivy cells may be strongly driven by CA3 afferents active during the late falling phase of the theta cycle.
source: suggesting that during theta oscillations in vivo these cells may be strongly driven by CA3 afferents active during the late falling phase of the theta cycle (Colgin and Moser, 2010)
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model results and supported by a citation.

claim: A clear majority of the interneuronal types in the model showed phase preferences similar to the in vivo condition where rhythmically discharging afferent inputs are present.
source: A clear majority of the interneuronal types in the model showed phase preferences similar to the in vivo condition where rhythmically discharging afferent inputs are present, indicating that theta-preferential discharges are to a large extent determined by the wiring properties of the CA1 circuit itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of model and experimental data.

claim: Theta-preferential discharges are to a large extent determined by the wiring properties of the CA1 circuit itself.
source: indicating that theta-preferential discharges are to a large extent determined by the wiring properties of the CA1 circuit itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The model only exhibited spontaneous theta oscillations at certain levels of afferent excitation.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, our strongly constrained model only exhibited spontaneous theta oscillations at certain levels of afferent excitation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A.

claim: When the excitation level decreased below 0.65 Hz, the theta rhythm fell apart.
source: When the excitation level decreased below 0.65 Hz, the theta rhythm fell apart
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A.

claim: When the excitation level increased beyond 0.80 Hz, theta power started to drop significantly as the oscillation frequency rose out of theta range.
source: and when the excitation level increased beyond 0.80 Hz, theta power also started to drop significantly as the oscillation frequency rose out of theta range (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Figure 6—source data 1–2), evolving into a beta oscillation (Engel and Fries, 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The synaptic-cellular organization of the CA1 circuit enables the intrinsic, within-CA1 generation of theta waves.
source: These data indicate that while synaptic-cellular organization of the CA1 circuit enables the intrinsic, within-CA1 generation of theta waves, the circuit is predisposed to exhibit theta oscillations only under particular excitatory input conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The CA1 circuit is predisposed to exhibit theta oscillations only under particular excitatory input conditions.
source: These data indicate that while synaptic-cellular organization of the CA1 circuit enables the intrinsic, within-CA1 generation of theta waves, the circuit is predisposed to exhibit theta oscillations only under particular excitatory input conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Under certain conditions the model network can oscillate at frequencies between 12 and 20 Hz.
source: The observation that, under certain conditions the model network can oscillate at frequencies between 12 and 20 Hz, is in agreement with recent experimental findings that rhythmic driving of septal PV+ cells can reliably entrain the hippocampus in a 1:1 ratio up to frequencies of 20 Hz (Dannenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the model that is consistent with experimental findings.

claim: Muting all the outputs from pyramidal cells caused theta rhythm to disappear.
source: When we muted all the outputs from pyramidal cells, theta rhythm disappeared (bar labeled 'Pyr' in Figure 6B), indicating that the recurrent collaterals of pyramidal cells play a key role in theta oscillations.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: The recurrent collaterals of pyramidal cells play a key role in theta oscillations.
source: When we muted all the outputs from pyramidal cells, theta rhythm disappeared (bar labeled 'Pyr' in Figure 6B), indicating that the recurrent collaterals of pyramidal cells play a key role in theta oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiment.

claim: Muting the CA1 pyramidal cell to pyramidal cell excitatory connections alone was sufficient to collapse the theta rhythm.
source: Interestingly, muting the relatively rare CA1 pyramidal cell to pyramidal cell excitatory connections alone (each pyramidal cell contacts 197 other pyramidal cells in the CA1; Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013) was sufficient to collapse the theta rhythm (bar labeled 'None' in Figure 6C)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C.

claim: Each pyramidal cell contacts 197 other pyramidal cells in the CA1.
source: Interestingly, muting the relatively rare CA1 pyramidal cell to pyramidal cell excitatory connections alone (each pyramidal cell contacts 197 other pyramidal cells in the CA1; Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013) was sufficient to collapse the theta rhythm (bar labeled 'None' in Figure 6C)
evidence: This is a specification from the connectivity data.

claim: Key roles for inter-pyramidal cell excitatory synapses within CA1 have been suggested for sharp wave ripple oscillations.
source: key roles for inter-pyramidal cell excitatory synapses within CA1 have been suggested for sharp wave ripple oscillations as well (Maier et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to experimental literature.

claim: Theta power dramatically decreased when pyramidal cell to pyramidal cell connections were either increased (doubled) or decreased (halved) from the biologically observed 197.
source: Furthermore, the parameter-sensitivity of the theta rhythm was also apparent when examining the role of pyramidal cell to pyramidal cell connections, because theta power dramatically decreased when these connections were either increased (doubled) or decreased (halved) from the biologically observed 197 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C.

claim: Silencing the output from PV+ basket cells strongly reduced theta power in the network.
source: Silencing the output from any of the fast-spiking, PV family interneurons (PV+ basket, axo-axonic, or bistratified cells), CCK+ basket cells, or neurogliaform cells also strongly reduced theta power in the network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Silencing the output from axo-axonic cells strongly reduced theta power in the network.
source: Silencing the output from any of the fast-spiking, PV family interneurons (PV+ basket, axo-axonic, or bistratified cells), CCK+ basket cells, or neurogliaform cells also strongly reduced theta power in the network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Silencing the output from bistratified cells strongly reduced theta power in the network.
source: Silencing the output from any of the fast-spiking, PV family interneurons (PV+ basket, axo-axonic, or bistratified cells), CCK+ basket cells, or neurogliaform cells also strongly reduced theta power in the network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Silencing the output from CCK+ basket cells strongly reduced theta power in the network.
source: Silencing the output from any of the fast-spiking, PV family interneurons (PV+ basket, axo-axonic, or bistratified cells), CCK+ basket cells, or neurogliaform cells also strongly reduced theta power in the network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Silencing the output from neurogliaform cells strongly reduced theta power in the network.
source: Silencing the output from any of the fast-spiking, PV family interneurons (PV+ basket, axo-axonic, or bistratified cells), CCK+ basket cells, or neurogliaform cells also strongly reduced theta power in the network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Muting S.C.-A cells had no effect on theta oscillations generated by the intra-CA1 network.
source: In contrast, muting other interneuronal types (S.C.-A cells, O-LM cells, or ivy cells) had no effect on this form of theta oscillations generated by the intra-CA1 network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Muting O-LM cells had no effect on theta oscillations generated by the intra-CA1 network.
source: In contrast, muting other interneuronal types (S.C.-A cells, O-LM cells, or ivy cells) had no effect on this form of theta oscillations generated by the intra-CA1 network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Muting ivy cells had no effect on theta oscillations generated by the intra-CA1 network.
source: In contrast, muting other interneuronal types (S.C.-A cells, O-LM cells, or ivy cells) had no effect on this form of theta oscillations generated by the intra-CA1 network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Partial muting of all PV+ outputs had a larger effect than partial muting of all SOM+ outputs.
source: In additional disinhibition studies simulating optogenetic experimental configurations, partial muting of all PV+ outputs (PV+ basket, bistratified, and axo-axonic cells together) had a larger effect than partial muting of all SOM+ outputs (O-LM and bistratified cells); see Figure 6D.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6D.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of PV+ cells, but not SOM+ cells, caused a marked reduction in theta oscillations in the isolated CA1 preparation.
source: Reassuringly, these results were in overall agreement with experimental data from the isolated CA1 preparation indicating that optogenetic silencing of PV+ cells, but not SOM+ cells such as the O-LM cells, caused a marked reduction in theta oscillations (Amilhon et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to experimental literature.

claim: Giving all interneurons a single electrophysiological profile created conditions that were not conducive for the appearance of spontaneous theta oscillations regardless of which interneuronal profile was used.
source: Surprisingly, giving all interneurons a single electrophysiological profile appeared to create conditions that were not conducive for the appearance of spontaneous theta oscillations regardless of which interneuronal profile was used (Figure 6E; note that the cells still differed in the strengths, distribution, and identities of their incoming and outgoing connections after this manipulation).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6E.

claim: Theta was not apparent in any intermediate steps nor in the final network where all interneurons had become PV+ basket cells.
source: Theta was not apparent in any intermediate steps nor in the final network where all interneurons had become PV+ basket cells ('All PV+B' in Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6F.

claim: Introduction of cell to cell variability in the resting membrane potential of interneurons in the 'All PV+B' configuration failed to restore theta.
source: Furthermore, introduction of cell to cell variability in the resting membrane potential of interneurons in the 'All PV+B' configuration at the biologically observed values for PV+ basket cells also failed to restore theta ('Var PV+B' in Figure 6F shows results with standard deviation of (SD) = 8 mV in the resting membrane potential; SD = 5 mV and SD = 2 mV also yielded no theta; biological SD value: approximately 5 mV in Tricoire et al. (2011) and 2 mV in Mercer et al. (2012)).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6F and supported by citations.

claim: Although PV basket cells appear to be important for theta-generation both in the biological and the model CA1 network, endowing all interneurons with PV basket cell-like properties does not lead to a network configuration conducive to theta oscillations.
source: Therefore, although PV basket cells appear to be important for theta-generation both in the biological and the model CA1 network, endowing all interneurons with PV basket cell-like properties does not lead to a network configuration conducive to theta oscillations (Hendrickson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: Muting the output from neurogliaform cells, but not the closely related ivy cells, affected theta oscillations.
source: We wondered why muting the output from neurogliaform cells, but not the closely related ivy cells, affected theta oscillations (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 6B.

claim: The model displayed spontaneous theta (and gamma) oscillations with phase preferential firing across the nine model cell types when excited with arrhythmic inputs at physiologically relevant levels.
source: When excited with arrhythmic inputs at physiologically relevant levels (see below), the model displayed spontaneous theta (and gamma) oscillations with phase preferential firing across the nine model cell types (pyramidal cells and eight interneuron classes).
evidence: This is a summary of the main results.

claim: These oscillations emerged from the network model without explicit encoding, rhythmic inputs or purposeful tuning of intra-CA1 parameters.
source: Consistent with experimental results (Goutagny et al., 2009; Amilhon et al., 2015), these oscillations emerged from the network model without explicit encoding, rhythmic inputs or purposeful tuning of intra-CA1 parameters (all anatomical connectivity parameters were exactly as previously published in Bezaire and Soltesz (2013)).
evidence: This is a statement about the model design and results, supported by citations.

claim: Cell type-specific perturbations of the network showed that each interneuronal type contributed uniquely to the spontaneous theta oscillation.
source: Cell type-specific perturbations of the network showed that each interneuronal type contributed uniquely to the spontaneous theta oscillation, and that the presence of diverse inhibitory dynamics was a necessary condition for sustained theta oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiments.

claim: The presence of diverse inhibitory dynamics was a necessary condition for sustained theta oscillations.
source: Cell type-specific perturbations of the network showed that each interneuronal type contributed uniquely to the spontaneous theta oscillation, and that the presence of diverse inhibitory dynamics was a necessary condition for sustained theta oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiments.

claim: The presence of diverse interneuronal types and the intrinsic circuitry of the CA1 network are sufficient and necessary to enable the isolated CA1 to oscillate at spontaneous theta rhythms while supporting distinct phase preferences of each class of hippocampal neuron.
source: In addition to characterizing roles for specific network components, these model results generally suggest that the presence of diverse interneuronal types and the intrinsic circuitry of the CA1 network are sufficient and necessary to enable the isolated CA1 to oscillate at spontaneous theta rhythms while supporting distinct phase preferences of each class of hippocampal neuron.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: These abilities may serve to maintain the stability and robustness of the theta oscillation mechanism as it operates in vivo in diverse behavioral states.
source: These abilities may serve to maintain the stability and robustness of the theta oscillation mechanism as it operates in vivo in diverse behavioral states.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The theta rhythm is thought to be important for organizing disparate memory tasks.
source: The theta rhythm is thought to be important for organizing disparate memory tasks (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Hasselmo, 2005; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Siegle and Wilson, 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: A CA1 network which has evolved a predisposition to oscillate at theta and gamma frequencies may enable more efficient processing of the phasic input it receives in vivo.
source: and a CA1 network which has evolved a predisposition to oscillate at theta and gamma frequencies may enable more efficient processing of the phasic input it receives in vivo (Akam and Kullmann, 2012; Fries, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations.

claim: Phase preferential firing may aid information processing tasks by providing order and allowing multiple channels of information to be processed in parallel.
source: In turn, phase preferential firing may aid information processing tasks by providing order and allowing multiple channels of information to be processed in parallel (Jensen and Lisman, 2000; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Schomburg et al., 2014; Jeewajee et al., 2014; Maris et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations.

claim: When the 454,700 stimulating afferents in the model are active at a Poisson mean of 0.65 Hz, they generate approximately 37,900 incoming spikes per theta cycle.
source: When the 454,700 stimulating afferents in the model (representing the CA3 and entorhinal synapses; calculated in Bezaire and Soltesz (2013)) are active at a Poisson mean of 0.65 Hz, they generate approximately 37,900 incoming spikes / theta cycle, given a theta frequency of 7.8 Hz (Equation 1).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the model parameters.

claim: About 4% of CA3 pyramidal cells fire up to four spikes per theta wave.
source: it has been estimated that about 4% of CA3 pyramidal cells fire up to four spikes per theta wave (Gasparini and Magee, 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to experimental literature.

claim: There are 204,700 pyramidal cells in ipsilateral CA3.
source: We previously estimated 204,700 pyramidal cells in ipsilateral CA3 (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013)
evidence: This is a specification from previous work.

claim: Ipsilateral CA3 provides an estimated 32,750 spikes per theta cycle to CA1.
source: giving an estimated 32,750 spikes from ipsilateral CA3 per theta cycle (Equation 2).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data.

claim: About 250,000 principal cells from ipsilateral ECIII synapse onto the CA1 region.
source: About 250,000 principal cells from ipsilateral ECIII synapse onto the CA1 region (Andersen et al., 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to experimental literature.

claim: Approximately 2% of ECIII cells are active per theta cycle at a low firing rate.
source: and approximately 2% of these cells are active per theta cycle at a low firing rate (Csicsvari et al., 1999; Mizuseki et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: ECIII cells could provide 5000 input spikes to ipsilateral CA1 per theta cycle.
source: Therefore, ECIII cells could provide 5000 input spikes to ipsilateral CA1 (Equation 3).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data.

claim: About 37,750 spikes per theta cycle arrive from ipsilateral CA3 and entorhinal cortex to the CA1 network in vivo.
source: Therefore, about 37,750 spikes per theta cycle arrive from ipsilateral CA3 and entorhinal cortex to the CA1 network in vivo
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data.

claim: The model has the capacity to process a biologically realistic number of spike inputs per cycle while maintaining the theta rhythm.
source: Thus, the model has the capacity to process a biologically realistic number of spike inputs per cycle while maintaining the theta rhythm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing model parameters to biological estimates.

claim: The modeling results unexpectedly revealed that interneuronal diversity itself may also be important in theta generation.
source: In addition, the simulations unexpectedly revealed that interneuronal diversity itself may also be important in theta generation, since conversion of all interneurons into fast spiking PV+ basket cells did not result in a network that was conducive for the emergence of theta, in spite of the key role of the PV+ basket cells in hippocampal oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiments.

claim: GABA_B receptors play a role in setting of spike timing of neuron types during theta.
source: setting of spike timing of neuron types during theta (Kohl and Paulsen, 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to experimental literature.

claim: GABA_B receptors play a role in cortical oscillations and memory processes.
source: and playing a role in cortical oscillations and memory processes (Craig and McBain, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to experimental literature.

claim: The relatively rare pyramidal cell to pyramidal cell local excitatory connections were required for theta generation in the model of the isolated CA1 network.
source: While it may be expected that isolated theta generation would require local pyramidal cells to provide rhythmic, recurrent excitation to interneurons, our simulations additionally showed that the relatively rare pyramidal cell to pyramidal cell local excitatory connections were also required.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiments.

claim: Pyramidal cells preferentially discharge at the trough of the LFP analog, strongly recruiting especially the PV+ basket and bistratified cells.
source: Pyramidal cells preferentially discharge at the trough of the LFP analog, strongly recruiting especially the PV+ basket and bistratified cells (green and brown raster plots in Figure 3C)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PV+ basket and bistratified cells cause a silencing of the pyramidal cells for about the first third of the rising half of the LFP analog theta cycle.
source: which, in turn, cause a silencing of the pyramidal cells (blue raster plot in Figure 3C) for about the first third of the rising half (i.e., from 0° to about 60°) of the LFP analog theta cycle.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: As the pyramidal cells begin to emerge from the period of strong inhibition, initially only a few, then progressively more and more pyramidal cells reach firing threshold, culminating in the highest firing probability at the theta trough.
source: As the pyramidal cells begin to emerge from this period of strong inhibition, initially only a few, then progressively more and more pyramidal cells reach firing threshold, culminating in the highest firing probability at the theta trough, completing the cycle.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: The progressive recruitment of pyramidal cells during the theta cycle appears to be paced according to gamma.
source: The progressive recruitment of pyramidal cells during the theta cycle appears to be paced according to gamma (see blue raster plot in Figure 3C)
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The intra-CA1 collaterals of the discharging pyramidal cells likely play key roles in the step-wise (gamma-paced) recruitment of more and more pyramidal cells as the cycle approaches the following trough.
source: and it is likely that the intra-CA1 collaterals of the discharging pyramidal cells play key roles in the step-wise (gamma-paced) recruitment of more and more pyramidal cells as the cycle approaches the following trough.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results.

claim: The model represented the isolated CA1 network.
source: Because our model represented the isolated CA1 network, the modeling results were compared with experimental data from the isolated CA1 preparation when possible.
evidence: This is a statement about the model design.

claim: Modeling results for which no corresponding experimental data were available from the isolated CA1 preparation were compared with in vivo data from anesthetized animals.
source: Modeling results for which no corresponding experimental data were available from the isolated CA1 preparation, such as the phase preferential firing of individual interneuron types during theta oscillations, were compared with in vivo data from anesthetized animals (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for comparing model results to experimental data.

claim: Experimental results from anesthetized animals offered the most complete data set for phase preferential firing.
source: Experimental results from anesthetized animals offered the most complete data set (e.g., no experimental data were available on CCK basket cells and neurogliaform cells from awake animals, see Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of experimental data.

claim: The phase preference of the axo-axonic cell in the model (163°) was closer to the anesthetized phase (185°) than to the awake phase (251°).
source: Out of the four interneuronal types for which in vivo data were available from both the awake and anesthetized conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), the phase preference of the axo-axonic cell in the model (163°) was closer to the anesthetized phase (185°) than to the awake phase (251°)
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and experimental data.

claim: The PV+ basket cells in the model displayed phase preferential firing (357°) closer to data reported from awake (289°–310°) than anesthetized animals (234°–271°).
source: whereas the PV+ basket cells in the model displayed phase preferential firing (357°) closer to data reported from awake (289°–310°) than anesthetized animals (234°–271°)
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and experimental data.

claim: Bistratified and O-LM cells fired close to the trough in the model, under anesthesia and in awake animals.
source: In contrast, bistratified and O-LM cells fired close to the trough in the model, under anesthesia and in awake animals, potentially indicating the primary importance of pyramidal cell inputs in driving these interneurons to fire during theta oscillations under all conditions.
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and experimental data.

claim: The model is fundamentally a model of the rat CA1 in terms of cell numbers and connectivity.
source: While our model is fundamentally a model of the rat CA1 (e.g., in terms of cell numbers and connectivity; see Table 3 in Bezaire and Soltesz [2013])
evidence: This is a statement about the model design.

claim: Some of the electrophysiology data used for constructing the single cell models came from the mouse.
source: some of the electrophysiology data used for constructing the single cell models (Appendix) came from the mouse.
evidence: This is a statement about the data sources for the model.

claim: The experimental data on the isolated CA1 preparation were obtained from both rat and mouse.
source: In addition, the experimental data on the isolated CA1 preparation were obtained from both rat (Goutagny et al., 2009) and mouse (Amilhon et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: There is no reported evidence for major, systematic differences in key parameters such as the phase specific firing of rat and mouse interneurons in vivo.
source: Because there is no reported evidence for major, systematic differences in key parameters such as the phase specific firing of rat and mouse interneurons in vivo, we did not compare our modeling results with rat and mouse data separately.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The in vivo theta rhythm has been reported to be either atropine resistant or atropine sensitive.
source: In general, the in vivo theta rhythm has been reported to be either atropine resistant or atropine sensitive, where the former is typically associated with walking and may not be dependent on neuromodulatory inputs, while the latter requires intact, rhythmic cholinergic inputs (Kramis et al., 1975).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to experimental literature.

claim: The theta that emerged from the model most closely resembled the atropine resistant form.
source: Given that our model did not explicitly represent neuromodulatory inputs, it is likely that the theta that emerged from our model most closely resembled the atropine resistant form.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model design.

claim: Both forms of theta may benefit from occurring in a network that is predisposed to oscillate at the theta frequency.
source: However, it also plausible that both forms of theta benefit from occurring in a network that is predisposed to oscillate at the theta frequency, as the model network results suggested.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model results.

claim: The results from the strictly data-driven, full-scale CA1 model are consistent with those of earlier models that demonstrated the basic ingredients capable of producing emergent network oscillations at a range of frequencies in microcircuits and small networks.
source: Our results from the strictly data-driven, full-scale CA1 model are consistent with those of earlier models that elegantly demonstrated the basic ingredients capable of producing emergent network oscillations at a range of frequencies in microcircuits and small networks (Rotstein et al., 2005; Siekmeier, 2009; Neymotin et al., 2011b; 2011a; Ferguson et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to modeling literature.

claim: The modeling approach provides a full-scale option to advance recent studies of network activity propagation and information processing during theta.
source: In addition, our modeling approach also provides a full-scale option to advance the recent studies of network activity propagation and information processing during theta (Cutsuridis et al., 2010; Cutsuridis and Hasselmo, 2012; Taxidis et al., 2013; Saudargiene et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to modeling literature.

claim: Emergent theta and gamma oscillations and theta phase preferential firing are possible even as additional interneuron types are incorporated and the network is scaled up to full size with realistic connectivity including 5 billion synapses.
source: Here, we demonstrated that emergent theta and gamma oscillations and theta phase preferential firing are possible even as additional interneuron types are incorporated and the network is scaled up to full size with realistic connectivity including 5 billion synapses between the 300,000-plus cells of our network model.
evidence: This is a summary of the main results.

claim: The current CA1 network model can be developed into a whole hippocampal or temporal lobe model by replacing the designed CA3 and entorhinal cortical afferents with biophysically detailed CA3, ECIII, and septal networks.
source: The current CA1 network model can be developed into a whole hippocampal or temporal lobe model by replacing the designed CA3 and entorhinal cortical afferents with biophysically detailed CA3, ECIII, and septal networks.
evidence: This is a statement about future directions for the model.

claim: A previous dentate gyrus model built to study epileptic network dynamics was used by several groups to study disparate topics including epilepsy, network mechanisms of inhibition and excitability, simulation optimization, and modeling software.
source: Previously, we built a dentate gyrus model to study epileptic network dynamics (Santhakumar et al., 2005; Morgan and Soltesz, 2008) that was then used by several groups to study disparate topics including epilepsy, network mechanisms of inhibition and excitability, simulation optimization, and modeling software (Migliore et al., 2006; Gleeson et al., 2007; Hines et al., 2008a; 2008b; Hines and Carnevale, 2008; Thomas et al., 2009; Winkels et al., 2009; Cutsuridis et al., 2010; Jedlicka et al., 2010a, 2010b; Thomas et al., 2010; Tejada and Roque, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to modeling literature.

claim: The resource intensive process of designing a detailed, large-scale model is offset by its potential usage in numerous ways by a multitude of groups.
source: Our previous model has demonstrated how the resource intensive process of designing a detailed, large-scale model is offset by its potential usage in numerous ways by a multitude of groups.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experience with previous models.

claim: Future efforts will be needed to continue to incorporate experimental data obtained by the scientific community on additional, not yet represented parameters into the platform offered by the full-scale CA1 network model.
source: On the other hand, future efforts will be needed to continue to incorporate experimental data obtained by the scientific community on additional, not yet represented parameters into the platform offered by our full-scale CA1 network model, e.g., on cell type-specific gap junctions and short-term plasticity, neuromodulators, diversity of pyramidal cells, glial dynamics, cell to cell variability (e.g., [Schneider et al., 2014]) and others.
evidence: This is a statement about future directions for the model.

claim: The model can be run on the Neuroscience Gateway, an online portal for accessing supercomputers that does not require technical knowledge of supercomputing.
source: Importantly, the model can be run on the Neuroscience Gateway, an online portal for accessing supercomputers that does not require technical knowledge of supercomputing (https://www.nsgportal.org/).
evidence: This is a statement about the accessibility of the model.

claim: The model is public, well documented, and well characterized in experimentally relevant terms.
source: The model is public, well documented, and also well characterized in experimentally relevant terms (See Appendix and online links given in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement about the accessibility and documentation of the model.

claim: All the model configurations and simulation result data sets used in this work are available online.
source: In addition, all the model configurations and simulation result data sets used in this work are available online (Bezaire et al., 2016b) at (http://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/V4CEH) so the same simulations can easily be repeated with a future, updated model using SimTracker (Bezaire et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of model data.

claim: There is an increasing recognition in neurobiology that we must compile our collective experimental observations of the brain into something more cohesive and synergistic than what is being conveyed in individual research articles.
source: As highlighted by the BRAIN Initiative, there is an increasing recognition in neurobiology that we must compile our collective experimental observations of the brain into something more cohesive and synergistic than what is being conveyed in individual research articles if we are to fully benefit from the knowledge that we collectively produce (Ramaswamy et al., 2015; Markram et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: By assimilating our collective knowledge into something as functional as a model, we can further probe the gaps in our experimental studies, setting goals for future experimental work.
source: By assimilating our collective knowledge into something as functional as a model, we can further probe the gaps in our experimental studies, setting goals for future experimental work.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of modeling.

claim: As powerful new tools are gathering vast quantities of neuroscience data, the extraction and organization of the data itself are becoming a challenge.
source: On the other hand, as powerful new tools are gathering vast quantities of neuroscience data, the extraction and organization of the data itself are becoming a challenge.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of neuroscience.

claim: At least three large programs are undertaking the challenge of extracting and organizing neuroscience data: the Hippocampome project, the Human Brain Project, and NeuroElectro.
source: At least three large programs are undertaking this challenge: the Hippocampome project (for neuroanatomical and electrophysiological data in the hippocampus of mice; [Wheeler et al., 2015]), the Human Brain Project (currently for neuroanatomical and electrophysiological data and models of the rat neocortex, [Ramaswamy et al., 2015]), and NeuroElectro (for electrophysiological data from all species and brain areas; [Tripathy et al., 2014]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Comprehensive databases create the opportunity to build strongly biology-inspired models of entire networks, with all the cells and synapses explicitly represented.
source: These comprehensive databases create the opportunity to build strongly biology-inspired models of entire networks, with all the cells and synapses explicitly represented.
evidence: This is a statement about the opportunities created by data resources.

claim: Full-scale models are not subject to the connectivity scaling tradeoff wherein smaller networks have unrealistically low levels of input or unrealistically high connectivity between cells.
source: Such models are not subject to the connectivity scaling tradeoff wherein smaller networks have unrealistically low levels of input or unrealistically high connectivity between cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of full-scale models.

claim: Full-scale models are usable for investigations into an almost infinite number of questions at any level from ion channels, to synapses, to cell types, to microcircuit contributions.
source: In addition, such models are usable for investigations into an almost infinite number of questions at any level from ion channels, to synapses, to cell types, to microcircuit contributions.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of full-scale models.

claim: This approach represents a new strategy in computational neuroscience, distinct from and complementary to the use of more focused models whose role is to highlight the potential mechanism of a small number of network components.
source: This approach represents a new strategy in computational neuroscience, distinct from and complementary to the use of more focused models whose role is to highlight the potential mechanism of a small number of network components.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the modeling approach.

claim: The scale, flexibility, and accessibility of the strictly data-driven, full-scale CA1 model should aid the modeling of other large scale, detailed, biologically constrained neural networks.
source: The scale, flexibility, and accessibility of our strictly data-driven, full-scale CA1 model should aid the modeling of other large scale, detailed, biologically constrained neural networks.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the work.

claim: The current CA1 network model produces results in agreement with experimental data.
source: The current CA1 network model produces results in agreement with experimental data, but also extends the results to probe the mechanisms of spontaneous theta generation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main results.

claim: The model extends the results to probe the mechanisms of spontaneous theta generation.
source: The current CA1 network model produces results in agreement with experimental data, but also extends the results to probe the mechanisms of spontaneous theta generation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main results.

claim: The model provides specific testable predictions that enable focused design of future experiments.
source: It provides specific testable predictions that enable focused design of future experiments, as well as providing an accessible resource for the broader community to explore mechanisms of spontaneous theta and gamma generation.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the model.

claim: The model is a relevant resource for exploring the transformation of incoming spatial and contextual information to outgoing mnemonic engrams as part of spatial and memory processing.
source: Because the model is available at full scale, it is a relevant resource for exploring the transformation of incoming spatial and contextual information to outgoing mnemonic engrams as part of spatial and memory processing, and other pertinent network dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the model.

claim: The CA1 model was implemented in parallel NEURON 7.4.
source: We implemented our CA1 model in parallel NEURON 7.4, a neural network simulator (Carnevale and Hines, 2005).
evidence: This is a specification of the modeling software used.

claim: The model simulations were run with a fixed time step between 0.01 and 0.025 ms.
source: The model simulations were run with a fixed time step between 0.01 and 0.025 ms, for a simulation duration of 2000 or 4000 ms (except for Figure 6D where one simulation ran for 1600 ms).
evidence: This is a specification of the simulation parameters.

claim: The simulations were executed on several supercomputers.
source: We executed the simulations on several supercomputers, including Blue Waters at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at University of Illinois, Stampede and Ranger (retired) at the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC), Comet and Trestles at the San Diego Supercomputing Center (SDSC), and the High Performance Computing Cluster at the University of California, Irvine.
evidence: This is a specification of the computational resources used.

claim: The CA1 network model included one type of multicompartmental pyramidal cell with realistic morphology.
source: The CA1 network model included one type of multicompartmental pyramidal cell with realistic morphology and eight types of interneurons with simplified morphology
evidence: This is a specification of the model design.

claim: The CA1 network model included eight types of interneurons with simplified morphology.
source: The CA1 network model included one type of multicompartmental pyramidal cell with realistic morphology and eight types of interneurons with simplified morphology, including PV+ basket cells, CCK+ basket cells, bistratified cells, axo-axonic cells, O-LM cells, Schaffer Collateral-associated cells, neurogliaform cells, and ivy cells.
evidence: This is a specification of the model design.

claim: The synaptic connections were implemented using double exponential mechanisms to better fit experimental data on rise and decay time constants.
source: The synaptic connections were implemented using double exponential mechanisms to better fit experimental data on rise and decay time constants.
evidence: This is a specification of the model design.

claim: All model results, characterizations, and experimental comparisons are publicly available.
source: All model results, characterizations, and experimental comparisons are publicly available.
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of model data.
